name: Applied Cryptography
description: Practical cryptographic constructions, attacks on deployed crypto, and crypto engineering.

ndss.narrative:
Applied cryptography at NDSS has long bridged theory and real deployable systems. The earliest papers in this dataset tackled high-impact practical problems: A Security Analysis of Honeywords (NDSS 2018) dissected the assumptions behind decoy-password schemes, exposing flaws that attracted widespread follow-on work, while ZeroTrace (NDSS 2018) showed how Intel SGX can be used to construct oblivious RAM primitives that resist access-pattern leakage in untrusted cloud settings.

The 2019–2021 wave brought a surge of work on oblivious and searchable data structures. Anonymous Multi-Hop Locks for Blockchain Scalability and Interoperability (NDSS 2019) introduced privacy-preserving payment-channel routing; meanwhile ORAM variants and searchable-encryption schemes with forward and backward privacy (Practical Non-Interactive Searchable Encryption with Forward and Backward Privacy, NDSS 2021) sharpened the efficiency frontier, making these primitives viable for real deployments.

From 2022 onward the agenda split in two directions: post-quantum migration and secure computation for AI. The post-quantum track produced performance studies of PQ authentication in TLS 1.3, practical V2V cryptography (When Cryptography Needs a Hand, NDSS 2024), and automated post-quantum tunnels (PQConnect, NDSS 2025). The AI inference track produced BumbleBee and Secure Transformer Inference Made Non-interactive (NDSS 2025), moving secure two-party inference from laboratory curiosity to near-practical reality.

uss.narrative:
The earliest papers on this list, from USENIX 2018, set a tone that runs through the whole period: applied cryptography is less about inventing new schemes and more about finding where deployed crypto breaks. Several 2018 works attacked the machinery the internet already relies on. "Bamboozling Certificate Authorities with BGP" (USENIX 2018) showed that the web PKI's domain-validation process could be subverted by hijacking routes, while "Return Of Bleichenbacher's Oracle Threat (ROBOT)" (USENIX 2018) demonstrated that a twenty-year-old RSA padding-oracle attack was still alive across major TLS stacks. Alongside protocol attacks, this year emphasized implementation leakage: "DATA - Differential Address Trace Analysis" (USENIX 2018) and "One&Done: A Single-Decryption EM-Based Attack on OpenSSL's Constant-Time Blinded RSA" (USENIX 2018) showed that even constant-time code leaks through address traces and electromagnetic emanations, and "Efail" (USENIX 2018) exposed how email encryption standards leak plaintext through exfiltration channels.

Over 2019 and 2020 the field broadened from breaking things to measuring and protecting real systems at scale. "Protecting accounts from credential stuffing with password breach alerting" (USENIX 2019) and "in-toto" (USENIX 2019) reframed crypto as infrastructure for everyday account and software-supply-chain security, and "The KNOB is Broken" (USENIX 2019) extended the attack tradition into Bluetooth key negotiation. By 2020 two threads matured in parallel: attacks kept landing on widely deployed crypto, with "SHA-1 is a Shambles" (USENIX 2020) producing the first chosen-prefix collision on SHA-1 and "Call Me Maybe: ReVoLTE" (USENIX 2020) eavesdropping on encrypted LTE calls, while constructive work like "Pancake: Frequency Smoothing for Encrypted Data Stores" (USENIX 2020) and "Big Numbers - Big Troubles" (USENIX 2020) tackled access-pattern leakage and systematic nonce leakage in (EC)DSA.

From 2021 onward the center of gravity shifted toward two newer engines: zero-knowledge proofs and privacy-preserving computation over real data. "Poseidon: A New Hash Function for Zero-Knowledge Proof Systems" (USENIX 2021), by far the most cited paper on this list, signaled how central SNARK/STARK-friendly primitives had become, a line continued by "Eos: Efficient Private Delegation of zkSNARK Provers" (USENIX 2023). At the same time, private set intersection and private information retrieval moved from theory to deployable tools in "Fuzzy Labeled Private Set Intersection" (USENIX 2021), "Constant-weight PIR" (USENIX 2022), and "Efficient Unbalanced Private Set Intersection Cardinality" (USENIX 2023). Meanwhile the side-channel and protocol-audit traditions never went away but climbed the hardware stack and into shipped products, with "CIPHERLEAKS" (USENIX 2021) attacking AMD SEV's ciphertext channel, "Three Lessons From Threema" (USENIX 2023) cryptanalyzing a popular messenger, and "GoFetch" (USENIX 2024) defeating constant-time implementations through data-memory-dependent prefetchers. The throughline is clear: the area now spans rigorous cryptanalysis of deployed systems on one side and engineering practical advanced primitives like ZK proofs and PSI/PIR on the other.

top4.narrative:
The earliest cluster here (2018) shows applied cryptography pulling in two directions at once. On one side, researchers were hardening the crypto we already deploy: "Return Of Bleichenbacher's Oracle Threat (ROBOT)" (USENIX 2018) showed a two-decade-old RSA PKCS#1 padding-oracle attack was still alive across major TLS stacks, "One&Done" (USENIX 2018) extracted RSA keys from a single decryption via electromagnetic side channels, and "Bamboozling Certificate Authorities with BGP" (USENIX 2018) attacked the PKI itself by hijacking routes during domain validation. On the other side, a wave of structured-encryption work both built and broke encrypted databases: forward/backward-private searchable encryption (CCS 2018, several papers) raced against reconstruction attacks like "Improved Reconstruction Attacks on Encrypted Data Using Range Query Leakage" (S&P 2018) and "Pump up the Volume" (CCS 2018), a cat-and-mouse the field tried to systematize through statistical theory in "Learning to Reconstruct" (S&P 2019).

The biggest momentum, though, came from zero-knowledge proofs and the cryptocurrency demand that funded them. "Bulletproofs" (S&P 2018) delivered short range proofs with no trusted setup for confidential transactions, while "Doubly-Efficient zkSNARKs Without Trusted Setup" (S&P 2018) and later "Transparent Polynomial Delegation" (S&P 2020) and "Wolverine" (S&P 2021) kept driving down prover cost and removing the trusted-setup crutch. Blockchains became both consumer and motivator: threshold ECDSA exploded as a way to custody coins, from "Fast Multiparty Threshold ECDSA with Fast Trustless Setup" and "Secure Two-party Threshold ECDSA" (both 2018) through the multiparty and UC-secure proactive variants (S&P 2019, CCS 2020), underpinned by "Practical Asynchronous Distributed Key Generation" (S&P 2022).

By the 2020s the area had matured into a full engineering stack. ZK moved from primitive to platform with "ZEXE" (S&P 2020) enabling private decentralized computation and "zkBridge" (CCS 2022) making trustless cross-chain bridges practical, while "Poseidon" (USENIX 2021) supplied a hash function designed specifically to be cheap inside SNARK circuits. Crucially, the field also turned its tools on its own correctness: "Simple High-Level Code for Cryptographic Arithmetic" (S&P 2019), "CryptoGuard" (CCS 2019) for detecting API misuse in real Java code, and the field-defining "SoK: Computer-Aided Cryptography" (S&P 2021) reflect a shift from inventing schemes to formally verifying and safely deploying them. The throughline across all four venues is the same: take elegant primitives, make them fast enough to ship, then relentlessly attack and verify what gets shipped.
